This model takes into account the effects of synchrotron and pair production processes, as well as the influence of the solar magnetic field on the propagation of these photons. The model is based on a set of integro-differential equations that describe the evolution of the photon energy spectrum and angular distribution. The model is validated against existing observational data and is shown to be in good agreement with the observed properties of ultra-high energy photons in the solar system. The model is also used to predict the flux of ultra-high energy photons in the solar system and is shown to be in good agreement with existing observational data. The model is also used to investigate the effects of the solar magnetic field on the propagation of ultra-high energy photons in the solar system. The model is shown to be in good agreement with existing observational data and is shown to be a useful tool for understanding the propagation of ultra-high energy photons in the solar system.

Nonlocal gravity theories, which are alternative models to dark energy, have gained significant attention in recent years. These theories have been shown to be mathematically equivalent to modified gravity models, which are often formulated using nonlocal operators. However, the application of the "equivalence theorem" in general relativity has been a subject of debate, as it is unclear whether the nonlocal operators used in these models can be considered as constitutive connections. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between nonlocal gravity and modified gravity by examining the properties of the tetrads and connections in these models. We show that the nonlocal operators used in nonlocal gravity models can be considered as constitutive connections, which are consistent with the mathematical framework of differential geometry. We also discuss the implications of this finding for the interpretation of nonlocal gravity models and their potential applications in cosmology.

Building conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) for concurrent systems is challenging due to the inherent conflicts that arise from concurrent updates. To address this issue, we propose a design framework called Eliminate-Win, which provides a systematic approach to designing conflict-free data structures. The framework consists of two main components: a conflict resolution strategy that involves removing conflicting updates, and a transformation process that converts concurrent updates into conflict-free updates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework by applying it to create new CRDTs for sets, maps, and complex data structures, as well as by optimizing existing CRDTs.

This study provides an overview of the extensive functional genomic data available from the ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics projects, which have mapped chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and DNA methylation patterns across various human cell types. We examine the collaborative efforts of the ENCODE project, which have led to the development of comprehensive databases and tools for analyzing functional genomic information. We also explore the integration of this data with genome-wide association studies, which have identified numerous genetic variants linked to 18 human traits and diseases, including height, weight, and susceptibility to coronary artery disease. We highlight the potential of functional genomic data to elucidate the biological mechanisms underlying these genetic associations and discuss the challenges and opportunities for future research in this field.

In the context of general relativity, gravitational waves are predicted to be tensor waves, but alternative theories propose the possibility of additional scalar and vector components. To investigate the existence of these components, we introduce a novel test that involves measuring the gravitational wave's effect on the line length of a gravitational wave detector. This test complements existing methods that rely on measuring the detector's arm length changes. By comparing the gravitational wave's effect on the line length to the arm length, we can determine the presence of scalar and vector components. This test can be implemented using existing gravitational wave detectors and can be used to constrain the parameters of alternative theories of gravity.

Radio sources with complex structures are challenging to study due to the difficulty in obtaining reliable spectral and polarization data. To overcome this limitation, we utilized a stacking technique to analyze the spectral and polarization properties of compact dim radio sources across a range of angular sizes. By analyzing the spectral index and polarization fraction as a function of angular size, we found that both properties exhibit a dependence on angular size, with the spectral index steepening and the polarization fraction decreasing as the angular size increases. Furthermore, we found that the polarization fraction is correlated with the spectral index, with more polarized sources having steeper spectra. These results are consistent with the idea that radio sources with more complex structures have shallower spectra and lower polarization fractions. Additionally, we found that the polarization fraction is correlated with the source's morphology, with more polarized sources having simpler structures. These findings have important implications for our understanding of radio sources with complex structures and their evolution over time.

This study investigates the impact of stellar outbursts on the surrounding environment, focusing on the generation of shock waves in the surrounding medium. We examine the propagation of these shock waves, particularly in the context of the stellar envelope, and explore the implications for the behavior of the envelope and the formation of a blastwave. We also consider the effects of wave-induced shocks on the dynamics of the system and the heating of the envelope.

We introduce a novel concept called geometric modularity, which extends the idea of geometric Galois representations to include a broader category of objects such as polynomials, matrices, and differential operators. Building on this foundation, we establish a geometric Langlands correspondence, which pairs geometric Galois representations with geometric automorphic forms. This extension of geometric modularity is then applied to redefine geometric weight spaces and geometric Hecke operators, resulting in a geometric version of the weight space action and Hecke operator action.

In solid-state systems, the interaction between electrons and vibrations is commonly described by the electron-phonon coupling, which is typically treated as a static phenomenon. However, this conventional approach neglects the dynamic nature of the interaction, which can be better understood by considering the inertia of the vibrating components. By applying a model that accounts for the mass of the vibrating components, we can derive a more comprehensive description of the interaction, which reveals that the electron-phonon coupling is not a constant but rather a time-varying quantity. This dynamic nature of the interaction can have significant implications for the behavior of materials and devices, particularly in the context of ultrafast phenomena and quantum information processing.

$\tau$-tilting theory, a relatively new development in representation theory, has emerged as a natural extension of classical tilting theory. This new framework has been shown to be applicable to various categories, including module categories of finite-dimensional algebras and coherent categories. This introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory will cover its fundamental concepts, including $\tau$-rigid modules, support $\tau$-tilting modules, and their connections to other areas of representation theory.

Conversational interactions are characterized by a diverse range of linguistic expressions, yet current dialogue systems primarily focus on syntactic patterns. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel Natural Language Inference (NLI) task that evaluates semantic variety in conversation. This task is designed to identify semantically equivalent utterances, regardless of their syntactic differences. To facilitate this task, we introduce a new metric called Semantic Variety (SV), which quantifies the diversity of meanings expressed in conversation. We also develop a dataset called ConvNLI, comprising 10,000 pairs of semantically equivalent utterances drawn from 1,000 conversations. ConvNLI serves as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of various NLI models in detecting semantic equivalence in conversational contexts. Our experiments reveal that existing NLI models struggle to accurately capture the nuances of semantic equivalence in conversation, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

Automated driving systems are increasingly being used to monitor and prevent accidents, but their effectiveness in detecting accidents is limited. This paper proposes a new approach to identifying accidents in video footage captured by roadside cameras. The proposed method uses a deep learning model to analyze video clips and detect accidents, such as vehicles crossing lanes unsafely. The model is trained using a dataset of video clips and is able to detect accidents with high accuracy. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of video clips and is shown to be effective in detecting accidents.

Theoretical models of planetary and brown dwarf formation have been extensively studied, yet the processes governing the formation of rapidly rotating objects have not been fully understood. In this study, we developed a computational model to simulate the formation of rotating objects, taking into account the effects of rotation on the gravitational collapse of gas clouds. By varying the initial rotation rates and masses of these objects, we were able to determine the mass-shedding limits for rotating planets and brown dwarfs. Our results indicate that the mass-shedding limit is significantly higher for rotating objects than for non-rotating objects, and that the effects of rotation on the formation process can be significant.

The limitations of conventional amplitude calculation techniques in accurately reflecting experimental observations are being addressed by a novel approach. This method employs a combination of artificial neural networks and a specific algorithm to generate a highly efficient representation of complex integrals, which are commonly found in theoretical physics calculations. The proposed framework is capable of incorporating the effects of experimental uncertainties and theoretical inaccuracies into the final results, which are presented in the form of confidence intervals. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the analysis of the branching ratio of the B+ → K+μ+μ- decay, which is a critical process in the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

A new, comprehensive model has been developed to explain the behavior of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and their afterglows, based on the concept of a jet with a constant opening angle. This model is a significant improvement over previous studies, as it incorporates the effects of GRB evolution on jet dynamics. By using this model, researchers can now predict the brightness of GRBs and their afterglows using a single parameter, which is the fraction of energy in the jet. This model has been validated against observed data from 100 GRBs and their afterglows, and it has been found to accurately describe the brightness of these events. Additionally, this model has been used to predict the properties of GRBs that may be detected by future space telescopes, such as the Einstein Probe.

This paper introduces a new vertex partitioning approach for bipartite graphs, specifically designed to be fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the difference in partition sizes. Given a bipartite graph G with a specified vertex subset R, we aim to divide the remaining vertices into two sets X and Y such that X union Y equals the graph's vertex set minus R, and the graph's edges are contained within the union of X union R and Y union R. Our research shows that this problem can be efficiently solved using a polynomial-time algorithm relative to a fixed parameter k, where k represents the difference between the sizes of X and Y.

In the field of machine learning, the issue of skewed data distribution is a prevalent problem that can hinder the effectiveness of models. To address this challenge, researchers have developed various methods to balance data sets, including resampling, cost-sensitive learning, and ensemble techniques. However, these methods often require access to the entire data set, which is not always feasible in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we investigate the impact of data imbalance on incremental learning and propose a novel approach to address this issue in an imbalanced class incremental learning setting. Our proposed method involves a combination of calibration techniques and a novel loss function that is designed to account for the skewed data distribution. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of the impact of different calibration techniques on the performance of imbalanced class incremental learning models.

This research proposes a propellant-assisted bipedal robot design that utilizes a novel actuation system to achieve efficient and robust locomotion. The proposed design features a compact, lightweight, and modular actuation system that utilizes a high-pressure gas to drive the robot's movement. The actuation system is capable of generating high torque and power, enabling the robot to perform complex movements and navigate challenging terrains. The research also presents a control algorithm that utilizes a combination of model predictive control and reinforcement learning to optimize the robot's movement and balance. The proposed control algorithm enables the robot to adapt to changing environments and maintain stability during movement. The research also presents experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed actuation system and control algorithm. The results show that the robot is capable of performing efficient and sturdy locomotion over a variety of terrains, including uneven ground and obstacles. The research also presents potential applications for the proposed design, including search and rescue missions and exploration of hazardous environments.

Let K be a field and V a valued domain whose maximal ideal is m. If the residue map from V to its residue field k is complete, then k is isomorphic to the quotient field of V/m. This paper explores the properties of such valued domains, specifically when the residue map is complete.

CPU frequency has been steadily decreasing over the past decade, with the latest Intel CPUs operating at around 3.5 GHz. This trend is expected to continue, with future CPUs potentially operating at frequencies as low as 1 GHz. While CPUs are highly efficient at high frequencies, their efficiency drops significantly at lower frequencies. To address this issue, we propose HyperDegrade, a novel CPU frequency scaling technique that dynamically adjusts CPU frequency to match the workload's requirements. HyperDegrade achieves this by leveraging a hierarchical degradation approach, which allows it to efficiently scale CPU frequency across multiple levels. Our evaluation shows that HyperDegrade outperforms existing frequency scaling techniques by up to 15% in terms of performance per watt.

We investigate the possibility of the Higgs boson resolving the discrepancy between the Standard Model and experimental measurements of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. By considering the Higgs' interaction with muons and potential new particles, we examine the implications for the Higgs' coupling to other particles. Our analysis reveals that the Higgs alone cannot resolve the discrepancy, but a specific combination of new particles could potentially explain the observed difference. This scenario, however, would result in significant deviations from the Standard Model predictions for the Higgs' interactions with other particles, which could be detected in future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider.

This paper introduces a novel unknotting procedure for classical and welded links, which is based on the concept of a bridge move. We develop a specific class of links that are both 4-ball unlinkable and unknottable through a bridge move, yet cannot be transformed into an unknot through any other means. Additionally, we identify a criterion for determining when a welded link is unknottable, which is not applicable to classical links.

We establish that the rational function semifields of tropical curves have a finite set of generators over a specific semifield, which is a key step in proving that these semifields are integral over another semifield.

Furthermore, we provide an explicit formula for the Fox-Hatcher loop in terms of a Vassiliev invariant, specifically the type-three coefficient derived from the third term of the formal power series expansion of the Kontsevich integral.

Matrix multiplication is a fundamental operation in linear algebra, extensively used in various fields such as computer graphics, machine learning, and data mining. This study compares sequential and parallel matrix multiplication approaches, utilizing a sequential processor and a parallel GPU. The experiment involved generating random matrices of different sizes and measuring the execution time for both methods. The results indicate that parallel processing is more efficient for larger matrices, while sequential processing is more suitable for smaller matrices.

The proposed framework is based on a network of robots that are limited in their computational and communication capabilities. We've expanded the application of an infrared-accurate amplitude formula, initially developed for effective field theories with infrared divergences, to non-singular infrared limits in Quantum Chromodynamics. This breakthrough enables us to derive new results, such as the infrared limits of multi-loop amplitudes in N=4 Super Yang-Mills theory and the first non-trivial infrared structure in QED. Furthermore, we've discovered that the formula's validity is limited to the leading color approximation in QCD, and we've identified the underlying reason for this limitation.

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) is a privacy-preserving technique that enables multiple parties to collaborate on a shared machine learning model without sharing their raw data. However, VFL is susceptible to privacy breaches, as demonstrated by a recent attack that exploits the model's output to infer sensitive information about the data owners. This attack, known as a pragmatic privacy assault, is particularly concerning as it can be carried out by a malicious third party who has access to the model and the data owners' information. In this paper, we investigate the limitations of VFL in protecting sensitive information and propose a new defense mechanism that can mitigate the risk of pragmatic privacy assaults.

Nonparametric density estimation is a widely used statistical technique for analyzing data, with kernel estimation being a popular method. However, selecting an appropriate bandwidth in kernel estimation is crucial, as it significantly impacts the accuracy of the results. This paper introduces a novel approach to kernel estimation that automatically adjusts the Fourier transform's basis based on the data, eliminating the need for manual bandwidth selection. This data-driven method is shown to be more accurate than traditional kernel estimation methods, particularly in cases where the underlying distribution is multimodal.

This study presents a new approach to group representations, specifically for wreath products of symmetric groups, utilizing Cartesian partition. By leveraging Cartesian partition, we can derive induced representations of wreath products from the representations of its component groups. Furthermore, we apply this method to derive the character tables of the symmetric group S8 and S9, as well as the wreath product S4 x S4.

This paper introduces a novel geometric concept, the M\"obius scalar curvature stiffness, tailored for conformally flat hypersurfaces within $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$. We establish conditions under which the M\"obius scalar curvature stiffness remains constant for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ that are in conformal contact with the position vector field. Additionally, we demonstrate that the M\"obius scalar curvature stiffness is constant for certain types of $\varepsilon$-biharmonic hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$, including those that are conformally harmonic. Furthermore, we prove that the M\"obius scalar curvature stiffness remains constant for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ that are conformally equivalent to the product of two spheres.

Automated segmentation of cardiac structures from non-invasive imaging is a crucial step in analyzing cardiovascular diseases. Deep learning-based methods, particularly U-Net, have become the gold standard for this task. However, the performance of these models in rare congenital heart diseases, which affect 0.8% of the population, is not well understood. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of U-Net-based segmentation models in rare congenital heart diseases, specifically Tetralogy of Fallot and Transposition of the Great Arteries. We trained and tested these models on a dataset of 100 patients with these conditions and compared their performance to healthy controls. The results showed that the models performed well in segmenting the right ventricle, right atrium, and left atrium, but struggled with the left ventricle. The study also found that the models' performance was influenced by the presence of surgical patches and the overall anatomy of the heart. The study's findings suggest that U-Net-based segmentation models may not be suitable for rare congenital heart diseases without further adaptation and training.

This study expands upon the concept of deterioration models by incorporating a singular perturbation term, $\varepsilon\nabla u$, into the model. The model's formulation is based on a singular perturbation of the material's properties, which are represented by a function $a_\varepsilon$. The primary objective is to establish the convergence of solutions as the perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$ approaches zero, utilizing the framework of $\Gamma$-convergence. The analysis is conducted within the context of the Ambrosio-Tortori functional, which is applicable to a range of models, including those involving the $p$-Laplacian.

This research paper examines a wireless communication system where a base station transmits data to multiple users, some of whom use energy harvesting technology to power their devices from the incoming signals. The study focuses on optimizing the distribution of time and power to maximize the total data transfer rate, taking into account the varying needs of different users and the efficiency of energy harvesting. The research problem is divided into two parts: one where the time allocation is fixed, and another where it can be adjusted. For both scenarios, the paper proposes efficient algorithms to find the best solution. The effectiveness of these algorithms is demonstrated through numerical examples.

In the context of learning from data, a common approach is to train a model on a dataset and then evaluate its performance on unseen data. However, a more efficient method is to learn from a dataset and its associated labels, a process known as supervised learning. In this paper, we explore the concept of supervised learning from a unique perspective, referred to as "learning from all items." This perspective is based on the idea that each item in a dataset can be seen as a mini-problem, and the goal is to learn from these mini-problems. We demonstrate that this concept is applicable to various machine learning tasks, including classification, ranking, and representation learning. We also introduce a new algorithm, called You Should Observe at All Items (YSOAI), which is designed to learn from all items in a dataset. We show that YSOAI can be used to solve various machine learning tasks, and we provide theoretical guarantees for its performance. We also conduct experiments on real-world datasets, and we show that YSOAI can outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of extreme quantiles in the tail of a conditional distribution, specifically when a condition is met. We examine how the extreme quantile behaves under the condition, and also analyze the behavior of the conditional distribution's right endpoint and extreme value index.

Word sense clarification is a critical aspect of natural language processing,
which is essential for enhancing the performance of various NLP tasks.
Building upon the foundation of Huang et al.'s Word Meaning Clarification
model, we introduce a novel approach called GlossBERT, which leverages
Chinese Wikipedia glosses to enrich word representations. By incorporating
these additional sources of information, we aim to capture more nuanced
semantic relationships between words. Our experiments demonstrate that
GlossBERT significantly outperforms the original Word Meaning Clarification
model in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Multimodal procedural knowledge is essential for mastering complex tasks, yet its underlying principles are not fully understood. To address this knowledge gap, we developed a comprehensive dataset that captures complex multimodal procedural expertise by sequencing instructional guides. This dataset, consisting of 1000 unique tasks, is derived from 10000 randomly generated sequences of multimodal instructional guides. These guides are designed to be comprehensible to humans and machines, incorporating visual cues, audio instructions, and text-based guidance. To evaluate the dataset, we conducted a series of experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of the sequencing process in enhancing task comprehension. Our findings reveal that the dataset can be used to develop advanced multimodal procedural models and provide a valuable resource for researchers in the field.

The structural characteristics of complex networks are often described using probability distributions, but existing methods fall short in capturing the dynamics of sudden, large-scale structural changes. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that models the distribution of network alterations resulting from sudden events. Our method is based on the concept of avalanches, which represent cascades of events that occur in response to a single external stimulus. We demonstrate that our approach can accurately model the structural changes observed in real-world systems, including the collapse of the World Trade Center and the 2011 Tohoku earthquake. Our findings suggest that avalanche-scale distributions can provide valuable insights into the behavior of complex systems during sudden, large-scale events.

This paper introduces a novel class of orthogonal polynomials with respect to the Airy function, defined on the interval [0, infinity). These novel polynomials are shown to be related to previously discovered families of polynomials, including those by Berman, Calogero, and Fokas. A key feature of our new polynomials is their universality, which allows them to be adapted to various weight functions. A universality theorem is established, demonstrating that these polynomials converge to a universal form near the edge of their support. Additionally, a Plancherel-Rotach type asymptotic formula is derived for the polynomials.

The primary limitation of gravitational wave detectors is the need for high-frequency sensitivity, which is currently achieved through the use of sophisticated control systems. A novel approach, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, is proposed to enhance high-frequency sensitivity by directly measuring the differential motion of two masses in a simple, linear configuration. This design is capable of detecting gravitational waves in a specific frequency range, from 100 Hz to 10 kHz, and is proposed as a supplementary detector to LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA. A detailed analysis of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's sensitivity is provided, along with an assessment of its potential to improve the detection of gravitational waves when used in conjunction with existing detectors.

In massive MIMO systems, the number of base station antennas is significantly greater than the number of data streams, which can lead to non-intersecting visibility areas. This phenomenon can cause access protocol failures, as it prevents the base station from detecting all active users. To address this issue, we propose a new protocol that leverages the base station's ability to detect the presence of users in specific areas. This protocol is based on a binary hypothesis testing framework and is designed to minimize the probability of access failures. We analyze the protocol's performance and derive a closed-form expression for the probability of successful access. This expression is then used to optimize the protocol's parameters, which are found to be highly sensitive to the number of antennas. We also investigate the impact of the number of antennas on the protocol's performance and find that it can lead to a significant reduction in the probability of access failures.

This study aims to establish a framework for predicting the dust emission from planetary disks experiencing vertical shear instability. We developed a set of 2D radiative transfer models to simulate the dust emission in these disks, considering the effects of vertical shear on the dust distribution. Our models reveal that the dust emission in these disks is significantly affected by the vertical shear, resulting in a characteristic pattern of emission that can be used to identify the presence of vertical shear instability. We found that the dust emission in these disks is consistent with the observed properties of the disk around HD 10687, suggesting that this disk may be experiencing vertical shear instability. Our results provide a basis for further investigation into the physical processes driving the formation of planetary systems.

Recent research has shown that the Big Apple configuration, a unique pairing of neutron matter and neutron star matter, is energetically more favorable than conventional neutron stars. This configuration could potentially be the most stable form of compact stars. We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the Big Apple configuration, exploring its energy, radius, and tidal deformability in relation to the equation of state. We have also examined the possibility of this configuration existing in finite nuclei, specifically in the $^{132}$Sn nucleus, and found that it is unlikely to exist due to the influence of the surface energy. Furthermore, we have investigated the possibility of this configuration existing in neutron stars, specifically in the 2.33-solar mass pulsar PSR J0740+6620, and found that it is unlikely to exist due to the high tidal deformability required for this configuration to exist.

DFT+DMFT calculations were performed on SrMnO3 to investigate its atomic physics, specifically focusing on the p-d hybridization. A new DMFT approach was developed to incorporate actual frequency-dependent hybridization functions, which were derived from first-principles calculations. This method was used to examine the 3d photoemission spectra, which were found to be in good agreement with experimental data. The results showed that the p-d hybridization has a significant impact on the 3d spectral function, particularly in the high-binding energy region, and that the p-d hybridization strength is a crucial parameter in determining the material's electronic properties.

A Mølmer-Sørensen gate is a highly effective method for entangling trapped ions, and its performance can be significantly improved by reducing the time it takes to execute the operation.  To achieve this, we propose a new approach that involves simultaneously driving multiple trapped-ion motion modes with oscillating forces at different frequencies.  By carefully balancing the contributions of each mode, we can create a MS gate that is less sensitive to frequency errors, resulting in a more robust and reliable operation.  Our analysis shows that this approach can reduce the time it takes to execute the operation by a factor of two, while maintaining a high level of accuracy.  We also demonstrate that this approach can be used to create a variety of different entangled states, including GHZ states and cluster states, and that it can be used to create a universal quantum computer.

The structural transition in barium titanate from cubic to tetragonal form is a notable example of a ferroelectric phase transition. This transition is a critical area of study in condensed matter physics, as it is essential for understanding the behavior of barium titanate and other perovskite materials. Researchers have long been interested in the structural templates that form during this transition, as they provide insight into the underlying mechanisms that drive the phase change. In this study, we have used a combination of advanced imaging techniques, including atomic force microscopy and scanning transmission electron microscopy, to directly visualize the structural templates that form during the cubic to tetragonal transition in barium titanate. Our results reveal that these templates are composed of nanometer-scale regions of tetragonal symmetry that are separated by interfaces where the material undergoes a cubic to tetragonal transition. Our findings provide a detailed picture of the structural templates that form during the cubic to tetragonal transition in barium titanate and have important implications for the design of new perovskite materials with tailored ferroelectric properties.

A new class of highly correlated Dirac metals is proposed, characterized by strong interactions and a unique topological property. A theoretical model is developed to describe this material, based on a strongly correlated Hubbard model on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor hopping. The model reveals that strong interactions can lead to a novel topological phase, resulting in a strongly correlated Dirac metal. The model's predictions are further explored using a combination of numerical methods and analytical techniques, including a mean-field approximation and a slave-boson mean-field theory. The results show that the strong interactions can be overcome by a strong magnetic field, leading to a novel topological phase. The model's predictions are also compared to experimental data from a variety of materials, including cuprates and iron-based superconductors. The results suggest that the strong interactions can be used to engineer novel topological materials with a wide range of potential applications.

This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for understanding bimodal distributions, specifically focusing on the relationship between two modes. By analyzing the frequency and ratio of the modes, we establish a systematic approach to studying bimodal distributions. This framework is applied to investigate the mode frequencies and ratios in the context of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS) data. Our analysis reveals that the mode frequencies and ratios are consistent with the predictions of the standard model of cosmology ($\Lambda$CDM) at a high level of statistical significance.

We investigate the potential for the NA62 experiment to detect heavy neutral leptons in the mass range of 100 MeV to 1 GeV, by analyzing the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay. Our study reveals that NA62 will be able to set stringent limits on the mixing between heavy neutral leptons and muons, with a sensitivity of $|U_{\mu N}|^2 \sim 10^{-7}$ for a 1 GeV mass, and potentially discover these particles if the mixing exceeds $10^{-6}$.

A Sagnac interferometer is a device used to measure the rotation of a reference frame, and its operation is based on the interference of counter-propagating light beams. The spectral shift of the interference pattern is influenced by the rotation rate of the device. In this study, we examine the spectral shift of the interference pattern in a Sagnac interferometer, taking into account the Doppler effect and the phase shift caused by the rotation of the device. We find that the spectral shift is proportional to the square of the wavelength of the light and the rotation rate of the device. We also find that the spectral shift is affected by the direction of the rotation of the device. Our results are consistent with previous studies and provide a theoretical basis for the use of Sagnac interferometers in measuring the rotation of a reference frame.

This note explores the parabolic adjoint operation and its impact on Weierstrass segments and components of the nilfiber within the context of type $A$ canonical pairs. We establish a formula for the Weierstrass segment of the resulting pair and provide a method to identify the components of the nilfiber of the resulting pair.

This paper explores the relationship between non-toric $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties and Laurent polynomials, specifically those with terminal singularities. We establish a connection between the deformation theory of such varieties and the deformation of their associated fan structures. By leveraging this link, we develop a criterion for determining whether a variety can be deformed into a toric one, utilizing this method to classify a specific class of three-dimensional varieties.

This paper introduces SADRNet, a novel self-aligned dual face prediction network for 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction. SADRNet addresses the issue of inaccurate face alignment caused by the lack of correspondence between predicted 3D face models and input images. It employs a self-supervised learning approach to jointly predict 3D face models and face images from the models, allowing for the refinement of face alignment through the minimization of the discrepancy between predicted and input images. SADRNet also incorporates a dual network structure to handle the challenge of predicting 3D face models from both visible and occluded faces. It utilizes a single network for visible faces and a dual network for occluded faces, with the occluded face network trained to predict 3D face models from the visible faces and the occluded regions. SADRNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks for 3D face alignment and reconstruction, with a significant improvement in accuracy and robustness.

We propose a new type of spontaneously broken symmetry, where the translational invariance is broken, and the associated Goldstone modes are described by an efficient field theory. This theory is analogous to the Nambu-Goldstone effective field theory used to describe spontaneously broken internal symmetries. We demonstrate that this efficient field theory can capture the low-energy behavior of various models, including the cubic lattice and the cubic honeycomb models. We also show that these models exhibit fracton phases, characterized by immobile point-like excitations, and that the low-energy behavior of these models can be described by a rank-1 tensor gauge theory.

Inflationary models that generate large curvature fluctuations in specific regions of space could potentially account for the formation of primordial black holes. A novel approach is proposed to investigate this phenomenon by incorporating an $\alpha$-attractor inflation model with a quartic potential and a sudden change in the inflaton field's evolution. This approach involves the introduction of a step in the inflaton potential, which is designed to induce a significant enhancement in the power spectrum of curvature perturbations. The potential is then used to calculate the mass of the resulting black holes, which are found to be in the mass range of $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-7}$ solar masses. This mass range is consistent with the constraints imposed by the gravitational wave observations of the LIGO/Virgo collaboration.

This paper focuses on labeled ordered trees, which are trees with nodes marked with numbers from 1 to n, arranged in a specific order. We define the deepest vertices in these trees as those with the highest distance from the root. Our research aims to count the number of ways to label a given unlabeled tree so that its root is the node with the lowest number among its deepest vertices. We develop a formula for this count and apply it to calculate the number of ways to label a specific type of tree, known as a caterpillar, where its leaves are the nodes with the highest numbers.

The 2020 US presidential election saw a significant increase in mail-in ballots, which are counted using automated machines. This counting process is prone to errors, which can be mitigated through the use of informed OCR technology. Informed OCR leverages the fact that ballot images are typically captured in a standardized format, allowing for the use of deep learning models to extract data from the images. This approach has been shown to be more accurate than traditional OCR methods, which are hindered by the variability in ballot designs and the presence of noise. To address these challenges, we developed a dataset of 10,000 labeled images of election ballot totals, which can be used to train and evaluate informed OCR models. Our experiments demonstrate that these models can achieve high levels of accuracy, with the best model achieving 99.99% accuracy on the test set.

In the field of time series analysis, linear models are commonly used for forecasting due to their simplicity and effectiveness. However, a significant challenge lies in accurately estimating the model's parameters, especially when the number of parameters exceeds the number of available data points. This paper investigates the phenomenon of benign overfitting in a temporal linear regression model, where the number of parameters is significantly larger than the number of data points. By utilizing a novel technique called the double descent curve, we demonstrate that a linear model can effectively capture both the underlying signal and the random noise in the data, even when the model is highly over-parameterized. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework for understanding the model's performance in terms of its parameters and data points, and we validate our findings through numerical experiments.

This paper introduces a novel speech enhancement framework, Complete Attention Bidirectional Deep Learning (CA-BiDL), which utilizes attention mechanisms to address the issue of irrelevant information in speech enhancement. The CA-BiDL framework is designed to handle speech signals with a single channel, employing two bidirectional long short-term memory networks to capture temporal dependencies and an attention module to weigh the importance of information. The attention module is further improved with a residual connection to mitigate the loss of information. The proposed framework is evaluated on the LibriSpeech test-clean dataset, and the results demonstrate that the CA-BiDL framework outperforms existing methods in terms of objective speech quality metrics, including PESQ, STOI, and SI-SDR.

The COVID-19 pandemic has been exacerbated by the rapid dissemination of misinformation, which has been fueled by the widespread use of social media. This has been particularly concerning given the potential for dangerous ideas to spread under the guise of harmless content. One example of this is the use of popular music to disseminate harmful pathogens, as seen in the case of a song that was shared on TikTok and claimed to contain a deadly virus. This incident highlights the urgent need for greater awareness and education regarding the dangers of misinformation and the importance of verifying sources before sharing content online.

In decentralized energy markets, storage management is a critical aspect of self-planning for microgrids and buildings. However, the lack of knowledge about future energy prices poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose a cautious self-planning approach that leverages a robust optimization framework to minimize the worst-case costs. By utilizing a scenario-based approximation method, we can efficiently solve this problem and develop a robust decision-making strategy. Our approach is demonstrated through a case study of a microgrid, which shows that cautious self-planning can effectively reduce costs and improve reliability in the face of uncertain energy prices.

This research utilizes an attosecond XUV pulse to initiate an electron correlation process in neon, specifically the 2p to 1s decay. By measuring the momentum distribution of the emitted electrons, we gain insight into the time-dependent evolution of the system's wave function. Our findings reveal that the 1s2p configuration evolves into a superposition of 1s2p and 2s1p configurations, with the latter being a result of electron-electron interaction. Our theoretical model, which accounts for the time-dependent evolution of the neon 1s2p configuration, aligns with our experimental data.

This study examines the global atmospheric circulation patterns of a simplified Earth model, which lacks continents and oceans, and is influenced by a uniform heating source. By using a cyclogeostrophic balance, we analyze the circulation patterns across a range of heating strengths. Our findings reveal that at low heating strengths, the atmosphere exhibits a stable, uniform circulation pattern, whereas at high heating strengths, the atmosphere exhibits a turbulent circulation pattern. The transition between these two patterns occurs at a critical heating strength, which is determined by the atmosphere's ability to balance the energy input and the energy dissipated through friction. The results of this study provide a theoretical framework for understanding the global atmospheric circulation patterns of Earth and other planets.

The vast amount of data available on the internet has made it possible to train deep neural networks to excel in various tasks. However, real-world applications often involve scenarios where data is constantly changing, which poses a significant challenge for these networks. In this paper, we present a new approach to address this issue by leveraging the large-scale data available on the internet to train deep neural networks that can adapt to new information in real-time. Our method involves a novel form of continual learning that leverages the large-scale data available on the internet to train deep neural networks that can adapt to new information in real-time. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods on a variety of benchmarks, including the ImageNet dataset. Our results show that our method is highly effective at adapting to new information in real-time, which has significant implications for the future of deep learning.

This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the algebraic multiplicity of eigenvalues, exploring its algebraic, geometric, and topological aspects. It also presents novel algebraic and geometric perspectives, along with a thorough analysis of the limitations of the Jordan canonical form. The discussion is supported by illustrative examples and a detailed investigation into the shortcomings of the Jordan form.

A quantum system consisting of a cavity and a three-level atom is proposed for generating bosonic pairs and squeezing in optical fields, which can enhance the sensitivity of optical phase measurements. The system's ability to create bosonic pairs is demonstrated through the analysis of the average number of photons in the cavity and the detection of photon correlations. The level of squeezing is assessed using the variance of photon number and is found to be influenced by the optical phase. The findings show that the level of squeezing can be optimized by adjusting the coupling between the atom and the cavity, as well as the decay rates of the atom and the cavity. The results also indicate that the system can be used to generate bosonic pairs and squeezing in optical fields, which can enhance the sensitivity of optical phase measurements.

Researchers have been developing quantum bits based on phosphorus donors in silicon for several years, and this work focuses on a specific setup where two phosphorus donors are placed in adjacent silicon valleys. The study investigates the behavior of this system by using a theoretical model that accounts for the interaction between the electrons in the two donors, considering the movement of the electrons in the four possible directions. The model is applied to a system where the two donors are separated by a distance of 10 nanometers, and the results show that the interaction between the electrons can be controlled by adjusting the electric field applied to the system. The study also reveals that the interaction between the electrons can be used to create a type of quantum entanglement known as a Bell state, which can be used for quantum communication.

We have experimentally observed the quantum conduction of HgTe gapless quantum wells, which are composed of two HgTe layers sandwiched between CdTe barriers. By measuring the longitudinal resistance in a magnetic field, we found that the Hall resistance plateaus at integer multiples of h/e^2, indicating the presence of a quantum Hall effect. This phenomenon is attributed to the formation of a one-dimensional Dirac particle system within the HgTe quantum well, which is confirmed by the observed positive slope of the Hall resistance versus magnetic field curve.

This paper evaluates the performance of a novel adaptive collaborative NOMA protocol for vehicular networks, specifically designed for road intersections. The proposed protocol dynamically adjusts NOMA power allocation parameters based on real-time traffic conditions, enhancing overall network efficiency. A simulation study demonstrates that the adaptive collaborative NOMA protocol outperforms traditional orthogonal frequency-division multiple access and fixed power allocation NOMA protocols in terms of throughput, fairness, and reliability.

The deployment of dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) in 5G networks has gained significant attention due to its ability to adapt to varying traffic demands. However, the lack of a comprehensive scheduling framework for uplink/downlink subframe allocation in D-TDD 5G networks has hindered its widespread adoption. This paper proposes a novel scheduling framework for D-TDD 5G networks, which leverages a game-theoretic approach to allocate uplink/downlink subframes based on real-time traffic conditions. The framework is designed to optimize the allocation of subframes by considering the interference between uplink and downlink transmissions, as well as the efficiency of the transmissions. The proposed framework is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its ability to adapt to varying traffic conditions and improve the overall performance of the network.

The concept of irregularity in the Hall effect, specifically the irregularity in the Hall coefficient, is explored in the context of a fixed lattice of vortices. The examination of irregularity in the Hall effect is conducted by analyzing the relationship between the average and the root-mean-square of the local Hall coefficient. The examination of this relationship is carried out by utilizing the data from the thin films of BSCCO, which are obtained from the measurements of the Hall resistivity and the magnetic field. The data are then analyzed in the context of the vortex lattice, which is described by the Ginzburg-Landau theory. The examination of the data reveals that the irregularity in the Hall effect is influenced by the vacancy distribution in the vortex lattice.
