In 1912, the Kapteyn Astronomical Observatory in Groningen was established, with Pieter Johannes van Rhijn as its inaugural director. Over the course of his tenure, which lasted until 1940, van Rhijn significantly contributed to the development of the observatory, both in terms of its physical infrastructure and its research output. His work encompassed the study of stellar variability, the structure of the Milky Way, and the development of the scheme of selected areas.
This paper provides a streamlined proof of the fact that the mod p weight space for GL_2 over any finite extension of the p-adic numbers Q_p has no singular points at the Kummer points.

This paper delves into the isoperimetric problem for a class of functionals defined on the space of sets with finite perimeter in R^n. These functionals incorporate a curvature penalty term, specifically the H^1 norm of the reduced boundary. We establish the existence of isoperimetric minimizers for a range of values for the curvature penalty. Moreover, we demonstrate that these minimizers exhibit smoothness properties on a mesoscale, akin to those found in the classical isoperimetric problem.

This paper introduces a novel approach to training deep neural network models that are split across multiple machines, focusing on training data divided into regional segments. By employing a model-parallel learning method, we can train separate model components on each machine, which is particularly beneficial for large-scale models. However, this approach is hindered by the need to transfer model components between machines, which can be costly. To address this challenge, we propose a new training strategy that leverages the inherent structure of deep neural networks to minimize the number of required transfers. Our method is designed to be flexible and can be applied to various types of models, including convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method can significantly reduce the number of required transfers while maintaining high training efficiency.

This research paper focuses on identifying the location and severity of damage in self-sensing composite materials using electrical impedance tomography (EIT). To address the inherent nonlinearity of the EIT problem, a novel genetic algorithm is proposed. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments involving artificially induced damage in a composite material. The results obtained from the experiments are compared to the actual damage characteristics, revealing a high level of accuracy in predicting damage location and severity. The study also highlights the potential for using genetic algorithms in other applications where traditional optimization methods may be limited.

The concept of emergence, where complex systems exhibit unexpected properties not found in their individual components, has been extensively studied. This research delves into the concept of emergent intelligence, specifically in the context of neural networks. We investigate the relationship between the knowledge possessed by individual neural network elements and the collective knowledge of the system. Our experiments reveal that the collective knowledge of a neural network system can exceed that of its individual elements, but this phenomenon is not universal. Our findings suggest that the emergence of collective knowledge is influenced by the compatibility of individual elements' knowledge.

This research paper presents a novel approach to learning control policies in robotics, specifically focusing on achieving complex movements like walking and flying in a single trial. The proposed method utilizes a unique combination of limited data and side information to enable robots to master new skills quickly and efficiently. By leveraging a small set of demonstration data and incorporating prior knowledge about the robot's dynamics, the method can rapidly adapt to new tasks and environments. The approach has been successfully tested on a variety of robots, including a walking quadruped and a flying drone, and has shown significant improvements in performance compared to existing methods. The results demonstrate the potential of this innovative technique to revolutionize the field of robotics by enabling machines to learn complex movements quickly and efficiently.

This paper delves into the tensor representation of a Euclidean space, focusing on the geometric interpretation of tensors and the visualization of their components. The discussion is divided into two main sections. The first section examines the geometric meaning of the tensor components in Euclidean space, while the second section explores the visualization of the tensor components in a three-dimensional Euclidean space.

A new type of light particle, dubbed 'taste-altering light bosons', is being proposed to address the mystery of why certain neutrinos oscillate at a slower rate than expected. This particle is hypothesized to be extremely light, with a mass as low as 10^-18 eV, which would allow it to persist for a vast period of time. This proposal is based on the idea that neutrinos interact with light particles through a very weak force, which would allow them to influence the oscillation patterns of neutrinos. This interaction would also allow light particles to be detected through the use of highly sensitive neutrino detectors.

The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly impacted the education sector, causing widespread disruption and uncertainty. As a result, many educational institutions have shifted to remote learning, which has presented numerous challenges for students. This study aims to investigate the effects of remote education on students' ability to stay on course during the pandemic. The research methodology employed a descriptive design, utilizing a survey-based approach to collect data from 100 students. The findings indicate that remote education has had a diverse effect on students' ability to stay on course during the pandemic. The results suggest that remote education has both positive and negative impacts on students' ability to stay on course during the pandemic. The study's findings have implications for educational institutions and policymakers, who must consider the diverse effects of remote education on students' ability to stay on course during the pandemic.

We derive the primary Ward identities for the Toda conformal field theory associated with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_3$. This involves expressing the stress-energy tensor and the primary field in $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ as linear combinations of the generators of the algebra, and then computing the conformal correlation functions of these linear combinations by differentiating the conformal correlation functions of the generators. The resulting Ward identities for the Toda conformal field theory are derived from the conformal bootstrap equations, which are based on the conformal symmetry and the operator product expansion.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, which implies that their word problems can be solved using a specific method. This solution can be extended to certain classes of groups, including those with K(pi,1) finite properties and aspherical coverings of finite 2-type spaces.

In this study, we examine the thermodynamic properties of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes in the presence of a scalar field, and we investigate the relationship between the charge and mass of these black holes to determine the validity of the cosmic censorship hypothesis. Our analysis reveals that the cosmic censorship hypothesis holds true for a specific range of values, and we explore the implications of this finding in the context of the phase transition of black holes.

This paper introduces a novel paraconsistent and paracomplete set theory principle, which serves as a foundational concept for constructing a paraconsistent and paracomplete Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

This research focuses on analyzing ambulatory data from individuals with electrocorticogram (ECoG) implants, which are typically used to monitor and control seizures. The study aims to develop a method for classifying gait patterns and estimating step frequency from the data. The developed approach utilizes a machine learning algorithm to identify patterns in the ECoG data and predict the corresponding ambulatory state. The results demonstrate that the method can accurately classify gait patterns and estimate step frequency with a high degree of accuracy. The study also presents a comparison of the developed approach with other existing methods and discusses potential applications of the technology in the field of neuroprosthetics and seizure management.

The concept of entropy is fundamental to the field of statistical mechanics, and its applications span various fields, including machine learning and data analysis. Nested sampling, a powerful Bayesian inference technique, is capable of calculating entropy in a straightforward manner. This method is particularly useful in scenarios where the probability distribution is unknown or complex, and can be applied to both discrete and continuous variables. The nested entropy estimator is capable of handling non-i.i.d. samples, and its performance has been demonstrated through multiple test cases, including the calculation of entropy in the posterior distribution of a Gaussian model.

We examine how right-angled Artin groups can be broken down into smaller groups, specifically looking at right-exact sequences where the middle group consists of normal subgroups. We demonstrate that right-angled Artin subgroups can be uniquely identified by their Stallings foldings. Furthermore, we establish that right-angled Artin normal subgroups are finitely generated if and only if their corresponding quotient groups are also finitely generated. We also provide a criterion for determining when a right-angled Artin group can be expressed as a semidirect product of two smaller groups.

The brain's dynamic functional connectivity (dysf) is a complex, time-varying network that changes over time. Understanding dysf is crucial for studying various neurological disorders, but it remains a challenging task due to the intricate nature of brain activity. In this study, we propose a novel approach called Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity Estimation (D-DICE) to analyze dysf from multivariate time series data. Our method combines a deep learning model with an efficient connectivity measure to extract meaningful patterns from the data. We evaluated our approach on two datasets, one from healthy individuals and one from patients with schizophrenia, and found that our model outperforms existing methods in capturing dysf patterns. Our results demonstrate the potential of deep learning models in analyzing complex brain activity and provide a foundation for future research in this field.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a comprehensive representation of evolutionary history, encompassing phylogenetic trees and incorporating additional evolutionary processes like hybridization and horizontal gene transfer. Despite their relevance, phylogenetic networks remain underutilized in large-scale genomic analyses due to the complexity of their representation. To facilitate the creation of informative networks, various tools have been developed, each employing different methods to integrate phylogenetic trees and genomic data. To facilitate informed tool selection, we conducted a comparative analysis of popular network creators, evaluating their ability to produce networks with specific topological properties. Our study reveals that different tools yield networks with distinct topological characteristics, influenced by their underlying algorithms. To further support tool selection, we developed a phylogenetic network creator evaluation framework, which can be utilized to assess new tools and inform the development of more effective network creation methods.

This paper introduces an extension of the Elevated Order Techniques (EOT) for rapid iterative matrix inversion, which can be efficiently accelerated using GPU technology. Building upon the original EOT method, the proposed generalization allows for the inversion of matrices with a higher elevated order, resulting in a more compact representation and a reduction in the number of required iterations. The new elevated order is determined by the number of bits used to represent the matrix elements. The proposed technique is particularly beneficial for applications involving large-scale matrix inversion, such as image reconstruction in Computed Tomography (CT). The efficacy of the method is demonstrated through a comparative analysis with the standard iterative inversion technique.

The concept of scattering eigenchannels was initially proposed to analyze how light interacts with a material, focusing on the amount of energy absorbed by the material. This study expands on the original idea by developing a general framework that can be applied to any type of scattering, not limited to light absorption. We derive a set of fundamental relationships that describe the behavior of these eigenchannels across a range of frequencies, providing a basis for further exploration and understanding of scattering phenomena.

We investigate the effects of random disorder on the topological properties of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where the hopping amplitudes are randomly altered. Our study reveals that a specific type of disorder can actually enhance the topological phase of the system, leading to the emergence of a new phase characterized by a non-zero Zak phase and the presence of a robust edge mode. This phenomenon is observed in a model where the disorder is generated by randomly removing atoms from the system, and we demonstrate that the topological properties of the system can be controlled by adjusting the disorder strength. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for the creation of topological insulators in systems with random disorder, and they have potential implications for the development of robust quantum devices.

This paper explores the concept of isomorphisms between trimmed spaces, which are metric spaces with their distance function modified to be zero only when the points are identical. We establish a connection between isomorphisms and homeomorphisms, showing that the set of isomorphisms between two trimmed spaces forms a convex subset within the collection of all continuous mappings between them. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the set of isomorphisms is a closed subset of the space of continuous mappings, and that it contains a unique element when the trimmed spaces are compact.

It outlines the underlying principles of issue framework and its application in interpreting deep learning models. Quantum computing has the potential to revolutionize various fields, but its widespread adoption is hindered by the susceptibility of quantum systems to errors. To overcome this challenge, researchers are developing fault-tolerant quantum computation techniques, which involve encoding quantum information and correcting errors through complex operations. However, these methods are difficult to implement due to the intricate nature of fault-tolerant protocols and the need for precise control over quantum systems. In this study, we propose a novel approach that leverages machine learning to automate the creation of fault-resilient quantum circuits. Our reinforcement learning-based framework enables the development of a high-performance code generator that can produce error-correcting circuits with near-optimal performance. Our results demonstrate that our approach can generate code that outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency and reliability, and can be applied to a wide range of fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols.

In optical interferometry, measuring phase shifts is highly sensitive, and researchers have developed methods to surpass the standard quantum limit using squeezed light. This technique has been successfully applied in gravitational wave detection, but its practical implementation in optical interferometry has been hindered by the need for complex light sources. A new approach is proposed, utilizing a dual-cavity setup to achieve sub-shot-noise sensitivity with uncorrelated light. This method involves a single squeezed state in one cavity, and the proposal is supported by a theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

The PHENIX collaboration has analyzed direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions, focusing on the interplay between jet-medium interactions and hadronization. Researchers have examined the hadron spectra and shape of the associated hadrons, as well as the nuclear modification factor and elliptic flow of the associated hadrons. The findings reveal that the hadronization process dominates the hadron spectra in Au$+$Au collisions, while the jet-medium interactions have a more significant impact on the shape of the associated hadrons. The study also indicates that the nuclear modification factor and elliptic flow of the associated hadrons are consistent with each other, providing evidence for the interplay between jet-medium interactions and hadronization.

This paper introduces the concept of the universal Smarandache's sigma product of figures, which is a novel mathematical idea. It is defined as the smallest number that is divisible by all possible numbers that can be formed using a given set of digits. The study of this concept is limited to numbers composed of up to three digits.

The rise of cloud computing has significantly transformed the delivery of services, with major cloud providers offering vast resources to support applications. However, the performance of cloud networks can be unpredictable, with significant fluctuations in network conditions that can impact the reliability of applications. This study investigates the effects of network performance variability on the scalability of applications deployed in cloud environments. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that network performance variability can lead to significant performance degradation and reduced scalability of applications. Our findings suggest that application developers must take network performance variability into account when designing scalable cloud applications.

In a distributed learning scenario, multiple learning agents operate in separate learning environments and aim to minimize their individual losses. The agents are not aware of each other's losses or contexts, and the only shared information is the number of rounds. This paper investigates a specific type of contextual linear learning problem where the contexts are not shared, and the agents' losses are determined by a linear function of the contexts and an unknown parameter. The paper presents an algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $O(d^{1/3}K^{2/3} + K^{1/2})$ for $K$ rounds and a dimensionality of $d$. The paper also provides a lower bound of $\Omega(d^{1/3}K^{2/3} + K^{1/2})$ for contextual linear learning, and a regret bound of $O(d^{1/2}K^{1/2} + K^{1/3})$ for a non-contextual variant of the problem.

The rise of remote work has significantly impacted the success of Scrum projects, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates the relationship between remote work and Scrum project success, employing a multi-method approach. Initially, a systematic literature review was conducted to establish a theoretical framework, which was then tested through a survey of 100 Scrum practitioners. The findings revealed that remote work negatively affects Scrum project success, with team cohesion and communication playing crucial mediating roles. To further validate these results, a case study was carried out, confirming the influence of remote work on Scrum project success. This study contributes to the existing body of knowledge by providing a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between remote work and Scrum project success, and offers practical implications for organizations managing Scrum projects remotely.

The analysis utilizes data from the ALICE experiment, collected at a collision energy of 2.76 TeV. The event shape is characterized by the difference in the second-order Fourier coefficients, denoted as $\Delta v_2$, which is calculated for pairs of events. The analysis also reveals that the elliptic flow coefficient, $v_2$, is influenced by the event shape, with higher $v_2$ values observed for particles with higher transverse momentum. This paper introduces the Quaternion Linear Canonical Transform (QLCT) and derives its fundamental properties, including the inversion formula, key theorems, and related transforms such as the amplitude, phase, and energy distribution. Building on these concepts, the study establishes both average and instantaneous indeterminacy principles for the Quaternion Linear Canonical Transform.

In wireless networks, power control is a crucial technique for optimizing performance and conserving energy. A common power control method is binary power regulation, which is simple to implement and widely used in practice. However, the performance gain of optimal power control over binary power regulation in interference networks is not well understood. In this paper, we investigate the extremal benefit of optimal power control over binary power regulation in $K$ user interference networks. We show that the extremal GDoF benefit of optimal power control over binary power regulation is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This result is derived from two key findings: (1) the extremal GDoF benefit of time-sharing over fixed time allocation is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$, and (2) the extremal GDoF benefit of optimal time allocation over fixed time allocation is $o(\sqrt{K})$. These results are established by analyzing the extremal GDoF benefit of time allocation in $K$ user X networks.

In particle-resolved simulations, the time step size is typically limited by the smallest particle, which can significantly slow down the simulation. A multi-time-step integration method has been proposed to overcome this limitation, allowing for a larger time step size. This method has been applied to a two-dimensional simulation of a single particle colliding with a wall, and the results show that the multi-time-step method can accurately capture the collision dynamics with a larger time step size. The method has also been shown to be more efficient than a single-time-step method, and the results indicate that the time step size can be increased by a factor of 10 without compromising the accuracy of the simulation.

This article explores the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ for positive integers $a$, $b$, and $n$. It initially demonstrates that $n$ must be divisible by 3, then focuses on cases where $n$ equals $3m$. The article proves that for each positive integer $m$, there are at least three distinct whole number solutions to the equation when $n=3m$.

This paper presents a mathematical model of a hopping robot moving on a soft surface, along with a simulation model and an optimization approach for the robot's movement. The surface model is based on a nonlinear spring, and the robot's movement is simulated using a set of differential equations. Optimization is achieved through a combination of a sensitivity analysis and a gradient-based optimization algorithm. The results show that the proposed method can effectively minimize the energy required for the robot to hop on the soft surface.

We have developed a comprehensive model that incorporates meson elastic form factors and meson production in the $t$-channel within a unified framework. This model is based on the concept of meson elastic shape factors, which we have derived using a quark model that accounts for meson wave functions. Our approach has been applied to various meson types, including pseudoscalar, vector, and tensor mesons, and our results are in good agreement with experimental data.

The complex behavior of charged droplets undergoing electrohydrodynamic breakup has been extensively studied, yet the dynamics of the resulting aerosols have received less attention. This study focuses on the breakup of charged glycerol droplets, specifically examining the formation of an EHD fan and the subsequent aerosols produced. By utilizing a high-speed camera, we were able to visualize the droplet breakup process and the resulting aerosols in detail. Our observations revealed that the aerosols formed an EHD fan structure, which was influenced by the droplet's charge and size. Furthermore, we found that the aerosols exhibited a distinct pattern of movement, with some particles being propelled outward while others remained relatively stationary. This study provides new insights into the dynamics of EHD fan formation and the resulting aerosols, which could have implications for understanding the behavior of charged droplets in various applications.

Understanding negation is a fundamental aspect of human language that is often overlooked in the field of natural language processing. To address this gap, we introduce CONDAQA, a novel contrastive reading comprehension dataset specifically designed to test models' ability to reason about negation. CONDAQA consists of 1,000 questions, each paired with a corresponding non-negated counterpart, allowing for a direct comparison of model performance. Our evaluation reveals that current state-of-the-art models struggle to accurately interpret negated sentences, highlighting the need for more robust negation handling in NLP systems.

This paper introduces a comprehensive overview of the latest advancements in community detection algorithms, which are designed to identify patterns within complex networks. It also discusses the challenges and potential applications of these algorithms, and provides an in-depth analysis of the leading scalable frameworks for computing community structures in large-scale networks.

Quantum annealing is a method used to find the lowest energy state of a system, and it's crucial to understand the time frame in which the system reaches this state. This time frame is known as the quantum annealing interval. In this study, we investigate the quantum annealing interval and sudden quenching in a specific type of problem called the exact cover problem. We analyze the system's behavior in terms of its energy levels and how they change over time. Our findings show that the system's state can be divided into three distinct time periods, and that sudden quenching can be used to identify the lowest energy state of the system.

This paper introduces a novel approach to compliance verification in process mining, specifically for trace segments. We address the challenge of determining whether a process segment of a trace adheres to a predefined workflow model. Our approach involves aligning the process segment with the workflow model, and we propose two alignment methods: infix alignment and postfix alignment. These methods are designed to be computationally efficient, and we demonstrate their effectiveness through a case study and comparative analysis with existing alignment techniques.

We have developed a comprehensive theoretical framework to investigate the influence of screening on the electronic and magnetic properties of infinite-layer nickelates, specifically LaNiO$_2$. Our model incorporates a dual-band approach, accounting for both the two-dimensional and three-dimensional characteristics of the nickelate system. By applying a random phase approximation, we have analyzed the screening effects on the Coulomb interaction and found that the two-dimensional component of the band structure is primarily responsible for screening. This screening effect is found to be insufficient to explain the superconducting state observed in LaNiO$_2$ films. Our calculations also reveal that the three-dimensional component of the band structure is essential for the formation of the superconducting state.

This study focuses on the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation, considering hard potentials without angular cutoff, in an unbounded three-dimensional space. We establish the existence of a stable, long-term behavior for small initial disturbances near a Maxwellian distribution, demonstrating that solutions converge exponentially to this state over time. Our findings indicate that the rate of convergence is directly related to the rate at which the collision kernel's angular singularity increases.

The Cox and Munk wave-tilt statistics, originally proposed in 1954, have long been used to model sea surface roughness and wind speed. These statistics rely on the assumption that sea surface waves follow a Gaussian distribution, which has been widely accepted until recently. However, new research has shown that this assumption may not hold true, as sea surface waves exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics. This study aims to re-evaluate the Cox and Munk statistics by analyzing wave patterns observed from the Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI) instrument. The IASI data, which covers a vast area of the ocean surface, reveals that wave patterns do not conform to a Gaussian distribution, but rather follow a Weibull distribution. This finding has significant implications for the accuracy of wind speed estimates and the reliability of the Cox and Munk statistics.

This paper introduces a parallelized version of a software framework testing case selection algorithm, which was initially proposed by the authors in a previous study. The original algorithm is designed to identify the minimum number of testing cases required to thoroughly evaluate a software framework's functionality. The parallel version of this algorithm is developed to efficiently handle large-scale software frameworks by utilizing multiple processors. The parallelized algorithm is based on a parallelized version of the testing case selection criterion proposed by the authors in their previous research. The parallelized testing case selection criterion is developed by dividing the software framework's functionality into smaller, independent components, which can be evaluated simultaneously by different processors. The results of this research demonstrate that the parallelized algorithm can significantly reduce the time required to thoroughly evaluate large-scale software frameworks.

This study delves into the emotional impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on social media users, specifically focusing on Chinese microblogging platforms. By analyzing 1.5 million posts from Weibo, we employed a combination of machine learning and deep learning techniques to classify emotions in the data. Our findings reveal a significant shift in public sentiment, with negative emotions dominating before the pandemic and giving way to a more balanced distribution of emotions during the outbreak. Furthermore, we discovered that the pandemic's influence on emotional patterns varies across different user groups, with government officials and celebrities experiencing a more pronounced shift in sentiment compared to ordinary users.

The concept of adverse mapping was initially proposed by Allman and Rhodes in 2012 as a method to create unordered labeled phylogenies from ordered ones. This paper introduces the notion of unordered labeling for ordered phylogenies and defines the Tai mapping as an adverse map for unordered labeled phylogenies. We then establish the conditions under which a given unordered labeled phylogeny can be derived from a specific ordered phylogeny through Tai mapping.

We investigate the properties of a squeezed and displaced state in the context of the quantum harmonic oscillator, specifically the "Compass state." By analyzing this state, we demonstrate that it can be effectively represented within a limited range of Fock space, allowing for a more efficient representation of the state's wave function. We also establish a connection between the state's squeezing and displacement parameters and the number of photons required for an accurate representation. Furthermore, we derive a precise formula for the state's overlap with the vacuum state, which is essential for determining the state's purity.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a proposed mechanism that may explain the observed dust development in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. However, the VSI's impact on dust growth remains unclear. This study investigates the VSI's behavior in protoplanetary disks with varying dust properties, specifically focusing on the effects of dust opacity and dust mass. The results indicate that the VSI's ability to generate heat is significantly influenced by the dust opacity, with higher opacity leading to more pronounced heat generation. The VSI's ability to maintain stability is also affected by the dust mass, with lower mass leading to more stable conditions. The study's findings suggest that the VSI can contribute to dust development in protoplanetary disks, with higher opacity and lower mass leading to more pronounced effects.

This paper establishes a new Liouville theorem for complete, non-compact manifolds equipped with a specific type of curvature condition, namely, a lower bound on the Ricci curvature that satisfies a particular inequality involving the Hessian of a function. We then apply this theorem to demonstrate the compactness of level sets for complete manifolds that meet the same curvature condition and have bounded behavior for the function.

In the field of video action recognition, the challenge of handling unknown action categories has been extensively studied. While numerous methods have been proposed to address this issue, they often require a significant number of unlabeled frames to effectively learn new actions. In contrast, our approach, Dynamic Entrances, is capable of learning new actions from a single unlabeled frame. By leveraging a novel framework that combines a dynamic entrance module with a global mean pooling module, we enable the network to adapt to new actions without the need for additional labeled data. The dynamic entrance module allows the network to selectively attend to relevant features, while the global mean pooling module facilitates the aggregation of these features into a compact representation. Our method has been shown to outperform existing approaches on multiple benchmarks, including the UCF101 and HMDB51 datasets.

The General Relativity theory's gravitational predictions have been extensively validated through various tests, and the PPN formalism is commonly used to model gravity in other theories. The PPN parameter $\gamma$ is particularly significant as it influences gravitational light propagation and can be determined using astrometric measurements. The Gaia mission's high-precision astrometry has the potential to provide a more accurate value for $\gamma$ and its uncertainty. The impact of $\gamma$ uncertainty on parallax measurements is examined, and the resulting uncertainty is found to be negligible compared to other sources of uncertainty. The study also explores the potential for using $\gamma$ uncertainty to improve parallax measurements and the resulting uncertainty is found to be negligible compared to other sources of uncertainty.

Reducing the number of variables in complex nonlinear systems is a key step in understanding and controlling their behavior. This paper presents a new method for reducing such systems that is both fast and adaptable to changing conditions. The proposed approach uses a technique called the balanced truncation to identify the most important variables in the system, and then refines this selection using a data-driven method. The result is a reduced model that accurately represents the system's behavior and can be used for control and prediction purposes. The method is demonstrated on two different systems, including a complex chemical reactor and a simplified model of the human heart. The proposed approach offers several advantages over existing methods, including its ability to handle nonlinear systems and its efficiency in terms of computational resources.

A new type of stable solitary wave, called self-boosting soliton, is discovered in the context of nonlinear wave equations. These waves exhibit constant velocity motion and are characterized by a balance between nonlocal and local effects. The study reveals that self-boosting solitons can be formed through the interaction of a nonlocal component and a local component, which can be either a dark soliton, bright soliton, or a pair of rogue waves. The study also provides a theoretical framework for understanding the formation and stability of these waves, which are formed in the context of coupled Schrödinger equations with nonlocal interactions.

In recent years, machine learning has become increasingly prevalent in various applications, yet the training data used to develop these models is often highly sensitive. To address this concern, secure multi-party learning (SMPL) has emerged as a promising approach, enabling the training of models without compromising the privacy of the data. However, the current SMPL protocols are limited to scenarios where the server is trusted, which is not always the case in practice. To overcome this challenge, we propose SIMC 2.0, a novel protocol that enables secure training of linear models in a setting where the server is not trusted. Our protocol is based on a combination of secure computation and a new technique called "simulated client computation" (SIMC), which allows the server to perform computations on behalf of the clients while maintaining the privacy of the data. We have demonstrated that SIMC 2.0 is highly efficient, achieving up to a 100-fold speedup compared to existing protocols, and has been successfully implemented in a real-world setting.

The FAST telescope's exceptional sensitivity and resolution have enabled the detection of previously unknown neutral hydrogen clouds and structures within the M101 galaxy group. By utilizing the FAST telescope, we have identified two previously undetected neutral hydrogen clouds, one of which is located within the M101 galaxy group and the other within the M81 galaxy group. Additionally, we have discovered a neutral hydrogen tail within the M101 galaxy group, which is associated with the M101 galaxy and is likely caused by a gravitational interaction between the M101 galaxy and a nearby galaxy. These discoveries highlight the potential of the FAST telescope to reveal previously undetected neutral hydrogen clouds and structures within galaxies and galaxy groups.

Answering questions that require open-ended common sense knowledge is a challenging task for both humans and machines. While existing methods have made significant progress, they often rely on retrieving a large number of unrelated knowledge points, which can hinder their ability to accurately answer questions. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Coarse-to-Precise (C2P), which aims to improve the quality of knowledge retrieved during the process. Our method first retrieves a broad range of knowledge points through a multi-grained retrieval process, and then employs a semantic-aware reasoning module to identify the most relevant knowledge points for answering the question. Our approach has been evaluated on the StrategyQA and CommonsenseQA datasets, and our results demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a significant improvement in accuracy.

Comets are celestial bodies that contain a significant amount of organic compounds and water, which are essential for the development of life. The study of comets is crucial in understanding the chemical composition of the early solar system and the potential delivery of life's building blocks to Earth. Cometary spectra are complex and contain information about the composition of comets, but they are often difficult to interpret due to the presence of numerous emission lines. The study of cometary spectra is hindered by a lack of knowledge about the electronic structure of certain molecules, which are responsible for the observed emission lines. The study of cometary spectra is further complicated by the presence of molecules that are difficult to detect, such as oxygen-containing molecular cations. The electronic structure of these molecules is not well understood, and their spectra are often difficult to model. The study of cometary spectra is essential for a better understanding of the chemical composition of comets and the potential delivery of life's building blocks to Earth.

This paper focuses on resolving the problem of expressing any whole number as the sum of four squared integers in various types of global fields, including function fields over finite fields and number fields. We develop a general framework to tackle this issue and provide a method to determine the minimum number of squared integers needed to represent any given whole number within a specific type of global field.

The vast amount of data produced by modern spectroscopic surveys is hindering the development of comprehensive galaxy evolution models. To address this issue, researchers are increasingly relying on spectral cross-matching methods to identify and analyze galaxies within the data. However, these methods are often limited by the use of traditional techniques, such as template matching, which can be inaccurate and computationally expensive. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel approach that combines the spectral features of galaxies with the use of advanced photonic technology. By leveraging the speed and precision of photonic systems, we can efficiently extract the spectral characteristics of galaxies from the data, allowing for more accurate and detailed analysis of galaxy evolution.

Medication pair prediction is a critical task in the field of drug development, and it is often approached as a link prediction problem within a knowledge graph. This paper presents a cohesive framework that integrates various methods for scoring medication pairs based on relational deep learning techniques. The proposed framework is designed to be modular and adaptable, and it is evaluated using a comprehensive dataset of 1.2 million medication pairs. The results obtained from this evaluation are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this area.
This study introduces a novel It\^o-Wentzell type formula applicable to paths exhibiting H\"older continuity with an exponent less than one.

In recent years, federated learning has gained significant popularity as a means of training machine learning models from data that is distributed across multiple devices. However, the training process is often hindered by the presence of non-I.I.D data, which can lead to a decline in model performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Random Stroll, which enables the training of machine learning models from diverse data sets. This approach leverages the concept of random walks to create a more uniform data distribution, thereby improving the model's ability to generalize. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments on a variety of machine learning tasks, including image classification and sentiment analysis. Our results show that Random Stroll outperforms existing methods in terms of model accuracy and robustness.

The inertial wave turbulence theory, proposed by Galtier in 2003, has been extensively studied through numerical simulations, but a direct demonstration of its predicted energy spectrum has been lacking. This study presents a significant breakthrough by using a direct numerical simulation of three-dimensional rotating Navier-Stokes flows to prove the validity of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov inertial wave turbulence theory. The simulation reveals that the energy spectrum of the flow is consistent with the $k^{-3}$ scaling predicted by the theory, and that the theory's assumptions of weak nonlinearity and scale invariance are supported by the simulation results.

This study investigates the influence of mandatory mental health therapy on convicted individuals within the criminal justice system. Mental health issues are prevalent among offenders, and untreated conditions can exacerbate recidivism. By analyzing data from the 2015-2016 period in Los Angeles County, we examined the effects of a mental health therapy requirement on convicted individuals sentenced to probation. Our findings indicate that this requirement significantly reduces mental health symptoms among offenders, with the most pronounced effects observed among those with pre-existing mental health conditions. Furthermore, the study reveals that the therapy requirement leads to a decrease in criminal activity among offenders, with the most significant reductions seen among those with mental health issues.

A significant challenge in medical image segmentation is the scarcity of labeled training data. To address this issue, semi-supervised learning methods have been developed, which utilize both labeled and unlabeled data to enhance the accuracy of the segmentation. In this paper, we introduce a novel consistency regularization technique that leverages unlabeled data to improve the performance of the model. Our method is straightforward to implement and can be easily integrated with existing deep learning architectures. Experimental results on two publicly available datasets demonstrate that our technique outperforms the state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods, achieving a significant improvement in the Dice Similarity Coefficient.

The ATLAS trigger system at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a sophisticated system that filters the vast amount of data produced during particle collisions. It is comprised of two levels, with Level-1 (L1) being a hardware-based system that processes collision events in real-time. The L1 system is further divided into subsystems, with the jet trigger being one of them. Jet triggers are used to identify high-energy jets, which are significant in the search for new particles. The ATLAS L1 jet trigger system is designed to identify jets with transverse energy greater than 100 GeV, which are typically produced by new particles. The system is comprised of two stages, with the first stage being a hardware-based system that processes collision events in real-time. The second stage is a software-based system that processes the data produced by the first stage. The system is designed to be highly efficient, with a low rate of false positives and a high rate of true jet identification. The system is also designed to be highly flexible, with the ability to adjust its parameters in real-time.
